ARCP: A core bond holding with room to reach beyond plain vanilla: corporate bonds, government debt, mortgage and asset backed securities, mostly high quality. The plus is flexibility to hunt for extra yield around the edges, which adds a little more risk than a strict core fund.
ARMS: Income bonds from many corners of the market: company bonds of all credit grades, mortgage and asset backed bonds, and government debt, picked actively by the manager. Spreading across sectors aims for a higher yield than plain core bond funds, with more credit risk riding along.
BD: A core plus bond portfolio built mainly on US government debt and agency mortgage securities, with corporate and other bonds added to lift income. It is meant to anchor a portfolio with steady interest, while the plus side flexibility reaches for a bit more yield than a plain core fund.
BSTP: Options on a large US stock fund, set for one year at a time, that can step its loss protection up to a higher level if stocks climb during the year. It is built for investors who want a cushion against drops that improves after gains, in exchange for capped upside.
CBLS: Stocks picked for strong finances and low prices, paired with short positions that bet against other stocks, so the fund is hedged rather than fully exposed to the market. The long short mix aims for steadier, stock picking driven returns, and it holds a large cash cushion from its short sales.
CNAV: About fifty US stocks chosen by a quantitative model that reads price momentum across the sub industries of the large stock market, currently leaning heavily into technology hardware. It tactically chases whichever corners of the market are rising, so its mix can change fast and it can whipsaw in choppy markets.
CPSM: Options on the S&P 500 set up each May for a one year outcome period, designed to guard against losses on large US stocks while keeping a capped share of any gains. It suits investors who want stock market exposure with the downside planned in advance, accepting that strong rallies will pass it by.
DDFF: Options on the S&P 500 built to gain from moves in either direction over a one year period starting each February, up to a limit on down moves, while absorbing the first 15 percent of losses. It is a defined outcome holding for investors who want some return even if stocks drift down.
DEED: Bonds backed by pools of loans and mortgages: home loans, commercial property loans, asset backed securities and loan bundles known as CLOs, with at least half government backed. It aims for income with a quality tilt, and stands apart by staying in securitized debt rather than plain company bonds.
EASY: Dividend paying US companies chosen for long records of raising their payouts, with health care the biggest slice at about a quarter, plus consumer staples, industrials and utilities. It is a defensive stock holding meant to grow income steadily while swinging less than growth heavy funds.
EHLS: US stocks held both ways at once: a full book of long positions plus a shifting set of short bets against stocks the manager's algorithm expects to lag, from 10 to 90 percent of the fund. The hedge aims to smooth returns and rely less on the market's direction.
EMC: Emerging market companies chosen for exposure to the rising consumer class, though in practice chipmakers and other tech hardware firms are the biggest slice, with banks next. It is a growth bet on shoppers in countries like China, Taiwan and Korea, held mostly through large well known companies.
FLAX: Large and mid sized companies across Asia with Japan left out, led by Taiwan and Korea, where chipmakers make technology nearly half the fund. It is a growth leaning bet on Asia's tech supply chain, with banks and consumer companies filling most of the rest.
FSCS: Small and mid sized US companies picked for strong balance sheets and steady dividends, spread across banks, industrial firms, insurers and food companies in near equal weights. The focus on financially sturdy payers makes it a defensive way to own smaller companies, favoring steadiness over fast growth.
GRNI: Large US companies picked from a well known market commentator's favorite themes, with technology about a third and industrials next, plus options strategies layered on for cash payouts. It blends growth stock picking with income, so it gives up some upside to pay distributions along the way.
GTND: Two big stock funds, one growth heavy and one broad market, with the mix between them steered by a trend following signal that can shift toward defense when prices weaken. It plays goalie for a stock portfolio: staying invested in uptrends, but ready to give up gains to limit losses.
HARD: Commodity futures covering energy, metals and farm goods, positioned by price trends so it can lean into rising markets and step back from falling ones. It packages that exposure without a K-1 tax form, which makes it simpler to hold than older commodity funds.
HIGH: Short dated US Treasury securities form the base, and an options overlay on top aims to add extra income beyond what the bonds alone pay. The result targets steady payouts with limited interest rate risk, though the options add complexity and can trim returns in some markets.
ISMF: Futures contracts across stock markets, bonds, currencies and commodities, traded long or short by following price trends wherever they appear around the world. Because it can profit from falling as well as rising prices, it is meant to diversify a portfolio and often holds up when stocks struggle.
JULT: Options on the S&P 500 set each July for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 10 percent of losses while capping gains. Like other buffer funds it trades strong rally potential for a known cushion, and the clock restarts every July.
KJUN: Options on a small company stock fund, set each June for a one year outcome period that absorbs a slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. Small caps swing harder than large ones, so the cushion is the appeal, paid for by missing the biggest small stock rallies.
LCO: A contrarian mix picked by hand: a few dozen stocks the manager sees as out of favor, with technology, energy and materials on top, plus small helpings of bonds and metals. It goes against the crowd on purpose, so it can lag popular markets for long stretches before its picks pay off.
LQDB: Corporate bonds rated BBB, the lowest rung of investment grade, issued by banks, carmakers, drug companies and other big borrowers across many industries. That bottom tier pays more interest than safer company debt, and it sits closest to junk status, so downgrades are the risk to watch.
MADE: US manufacturing companies: makers of farm and construction machinery, electrical equipment, engines, tools and factory gear, with industrials about three quarters of the fund. It is a direct bet on American factory output and the push to build more at home, so it rises and falls with industrial demand.
MDPL: Thirty US stocks in equal weights, chosen as dividend paying value stocks from a broad large and mid cap universe, spanning financial, technology, health care and other sectors. Equal weighting keeps any single company from dominating, and the dividend value tilt favors cheaper stocks that pay cash back.
MEMX: Emerging market stocks with China deliberately left out, led by Taiwan and Korean chipmakers, with banks the next biggest slice. It is a growth bet on the rest of the emerging world for investors who want that exposure without Chinese companies in the mix.
NBTR: A broad bond mix led by US government debt, with corporate bonds, mortgage backed and asset backed securities filling out the portfolio. It works as a core income holding, and managers can tilt toward whichever bond corner looks best, adding flexibility a plain index fund lacks.
NMAY: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big growth stock basket, set each May for a one year outcome period that absorbs a slice of losses in exchange for capped gains. It offers a cushioned way to hold tech heavy stocks, with technology over half the underlying exposure.
OCTU: Options on the S&P 500 set each October for a one year outcome period, cushioning the first 15 percent of losses while leaving gains uncapped once stocks climb past a small starting hurdle. It trades the usual gain cap for that opening flat stretch, a different shape of protection.
ONLN: Companies that sell through the internet: big e-commerce platforms, online marketplaces, car buying sites and pet and home goods retailers, almost all consumer discretionary. It is a concentrated bet on shopping moving online, so a few giant platforms drive most of its performance.
OZEM: Drug companies working on GLP-1 and weight loss treatments, from the two big makers of today's hit medicines to small developers still testing theirs. It is a concentrated bet on one drug boom, all health care, so it can swing hard on trial results and rival launches.
PBJN: Options on the S&P 500 set each June for a one year outcome period, absorbing the first 20 percent of losses while capping gains. The trade is certainty about the downside for that year, paid for by giving up strong rallies in large US stocks.
PEXL: About one hundred large and mid sized US companies in equal weights, screened for earning a high share of their sales abroad and for fast growing free cash flow. It tilts toward technology and global brands, offering exporters' earnings without leaving the US stock market.
PSFJ: Options on the S&P 500 in a flexible structured outcome design that starts each July, with room to reset the outcome terms during the year rather than locking them for a full term. It offers large stock exposure with a built in cushion, traded for a cap on gains.
PVEX: A defensive blend that keeps partial exposure to large US stocks through stock funds, while much of the money sits in Treasury bills and high quality bond funds. It aims to capture a good share of stock gains yet give back far less in sell-offs, playing goalie for a stock portfolio.
QAT: Stocks listed in Qatar, where banks and other financial companies make up over half the fund, with energy, materials and telecom behind them. It is a single country bet on a wealthy gas exporting economy, so bank earnings and energy prices drive most of what it does.
QVOL: Nasdaq listed growth stocks, technology about two thirds of the fund, with an options program that sells calls against the holdings to turn part of their upside into income. It targets frequent payouts from volatile tech names, accepting smaller gains when those stocks run hard.
QVOY: A fund of funds that rotates money among four sleeves: core stocks, actively picked stocks, bonds and alternatives, shifting the mix as its process directs. The appeal is one ticker doing the rotating for you, though the layers of funds mean its results trail whichever sleeve is hottest.
RHRX: A rotating basket of other stock funds: broad market funds form the base, with sector and industry funds like semiconductors dialed up or down as the manager's rotation process directs. It is active allocation in one ticker, chasing stronger areas of the stock market while trying to dodge weaker ones.
RIGS: A worldwide mix of income bonds: government debt, company bonds and other fixed income of many maturities, ratings and currencies, steered actively toward the best yield opportunities. It aims to be a flexible income core, reaching abroad and down the quality scale where plain US bond funds do not.
RSBY: Two strategies stacked in one fund: a core of US bonds, plus a futures program that harvests yield like returns from rolling futures contracts across markets, layered on top with borrowing. The stacking aims to earn more from each dollar invested, at the cost of leverage and complexity.
SQMX: Options on the S&P 500 in a quarterly design that aims for the deepest loss cushion available each quarter, resetting four times a year. Shorter outcome periods mean the protection and the gain cap refresh often, suiting investors who do not want to commit to a full year.
TMSF: Bonds from every sector that pays income: government debt, corporate bonds, mortgage securities and floating rate loans, with room to reach into emerging markets for extra yield. Managers shift the mix actively, making it a flexible income core that takes more credit risk than a plain index bond fund.
TRUD: Companies that sell discretionary goods and experiences: online retail, carmakers, home improvement stores, restaurants and travel, essentially the full consumer discretionary sector in one holding. It is a focused bet on household spending, so it shines when consumers feel flush and sags when they pull back.
TSYY: An income strategy built on options tied to Tesla shares, using contracts on a Tesla linked fund to collect option premiums that fund frequent payouts. It lives and dies with one very volatile stock, and its gains are capped, so it is an income play on Tesla rather than a way to own it.
WBIY: US companies screened for high dividend yields and solid underlying value, spread across industries like telecom, food, tech hardware and banks. It is built for income first, so the payout is the point, and the stock picks lean toward cheaper, cash rich businesses rather than fast growers.
WNTR: An options strategy that bets against MicroStrategy, the bitcoin holding software company, while selling options to generate monthly income from its wild price swings. It gains when that stock falls and loses when it jumps, so it is a hedge or speculation tool, not a steady income holding.
WOMN: Large and mid sized US companies rated highly for empowering women, through measures like women in leadership and fair pay and promotion practices, across technology, banks, health care and more. It keeps a broad market shape while tilting toward employers with strong records on gender equity.
XFEB: Options linked to the S&P 500 give this fund a set outcome for a one year period starting each February: it cushions a moderate slice of losses and boosts gains up to a cap. It suits investors who want stock exposure with a softer landing, accepting limited upside in strong years.
XRMI: Large US stocks across every major industry, paired with an options collar that sells calls and buys protective puts on the same basket. The collar turns part of the market's upside into monthly income and softens drops, so it trails strong rallies but falls less in sell-offs.
